title: "Data and measures"
abstract: "This chapter describes the data behind the analyses: parent-report vocabulary assessments of children with Down syndrome pooled from several international studies and harmonised onto a common 810-item reference inventory. For each study we tabulate the numbers of words understood and spoken — and, for the signing sub-set, words signed — by age, alongside the observation and child counts, age range, and per-measure summaries. It then documents the measurement decisions that shape those counts: the common 810-item scale and its relationship to each source form's native checklist ceiling, the production-only treatment of Wordbank Words & Sentences records, and the study-specific inclusion rules applied when loading the data."

## Data sources {#sec-data}

We pool vocabulary assessments of children with Down syndrome from several international studies, harmonised onto the common 810-item reference inventory described under [Measures](#measures). Each study contributes parent-report checklist counts of words *understood* and *spoken* — and, for the signing sub-set, words *signed* — together with the child's age in months. The table below inventories each study: the number of observations and distinct children, the age range, and the mean, median and quartiles of each measure (full detail in the accompanying CSV). The figures that follow plot the raw observations, one colour per study.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-ds-datasets
#| echo: false
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd

_p = Path("figures/descriptives/dataset_summary_ds.csv")
_ds_summary = (
    pd.read_csv(_p)
    if _p.exists()
    else pd.DataFrame({"note": ["Run scripts/generate_descriptive_report.py"]})
)
_ds_summary
```

## Measures

The models report vocabulary counts on a common **810-item reference scale** ($N_{\text{trials}} = 810$). The reference inventory is the DSE vocabulary checklists: Checklists 1, 2 and 3 list 120, 340 and 350 words respectively, so the full set is $120 + 340 + 350 = 810$ words. This is a reference-inventory scale rather than the native denominator for every source checklist: some source forms have lower ceilings, including Wordbank Words & Gestures (396 items), the Oxford CDI (416 items) and the MacArthur-Bates Words & Sentences form (680 items). The common scale keeps estimates comparable across DS and TD instruments, but it remains a modelling approximation, so source-form ceilings and near-ceiling observations should be checked when interpreting high-count regions.

Each source's native checklist ceiling is recorded in the data as `survey_vocab_max`; rows whose count exceeds their form's ceiling are dropped as impossible (data-entry errors) by the form-ceiling guard, but the likelihoods otherwise do not use the native ceiling. Univariate outcomes, understood counts and joint-model fallback rows use the common 810-item denominator, while paired logically nested spoken and signed rows use the observed understood count. A count near a small form's ceiling is therefore effectively right-censored under the harmonisation — a child who checks every item on Words & Gestures (396 items) records 396, which an understood or marginal likelihood treats as one of 810 possible words. The by-source/form counts of at-ceiling and near-ceiling observations are tabulated by `scripts/data_coverage.py` (`ceiling_by_form.csv`) so this exposure can be quantified. In the current data build the exposure is concentrated in the small-ceiling comprehension studies — the Oxford CDI (416-item) source and the MacArthur-Bates Words & Gestures (396-item) source — where about a fifth of comprehension counts fall within 90% of the native ceiling; most other source-and-outcome combinations have none. A dual-form crosswalk shows this harmonisation does not materially bias the estimates, and that the fixed-810 denominator is the right choice rather than a per-form one. The source CDIs are *nested*: the shorter forms comprise the earlier-acquired, more common words, and the items absent from a short form are the rarer words an ability-matched child is unlikely to know — so a short-form count entered against the 810-item denominator is close to the child's true full-inventory fraction, not a length-scaled deflation of it. The uk_02 study administered both the 810-item DSE checklist and the 416-item Oxford CDI to the same children; among those measured on both *at the same age* the median DSE-to-Oxford count ratio for words understood is 1.14, and a Bayesian equating model fitted to all 34 dual-form children (`scripts/crosswalk_dse_oxford.py`) puts the age-adjusted ratio near 1 at the ages where the short forms are actually administered, rising only mildly by school age. Fixed-810 implies a ratio of 1; a per-form denominator ($n_{\text{trials}} = \texttt{survey\_vocab\_max}$) implies $810 / 416 = 1.95$, which the crosswalk excludes across the whole range ($P(R < 1.95) = 1.00$). The fixed 810 denominator is therefore retained as a *validated* approximation, not a documented guess: a per-form rescaling would over-correct badly. The residual is a small, level-dependent undercount for short-form studies — near zero at the young ages where those forms are used, growing only at older ages where almost no short-form data exist — which the study-level random intercepts (VG07 onward) absorb as a level offset, leaving a mild effect only in the non-hierarchical baselines (VG01, VG02, VG05, VG14).

That nesting argument covers a source form whose *absent* items are the rarer words, but not an administration that omitted part of the reference inventory itself. The ie_01 baseline wave is such a case: DSE Checklist 3 (350 of the 810 items) is recorded as exactly zero for every child on all three response types (understood, imitated and said), no baseline total exceeds Checklists 1 + 2 = 460, and 33 of 46 follow-up records carry non-zero Checklist 3 counts of up to 328 — including children whose baseline total already exceeded 390. At matched vocabulary the follow-up wave puts about a tenth of Checklist 3 known against none at baseline, so the zeros reflect an un-administered subscale rather than ability. The baseline wave is therefore a 460-item administration: its recorded ceiling is 460, and its counts are masked from the analysis pool by default because they are not on the reference scale the likelihoods score against, and cannot be rescaled onto it (the omitted Checklist 3 items are markedly harder than the administered ones, so the proportion known on Checklists 1–2 is not the proportion known on all three). The 59 baseline rows are retained with missing outcomes so age coverage stays auditable, and the loaders accept `include_incomplete_administrations=True` to reintroduce them as a sensitivity. The ie_01 follow-up wave is a complete 810-item administration and is unaffected.

Down Syndrome Ireland's ie_01 comprehension counts are used as the parent reported them. An earlier harmonisation set ie_01 understood to the larger of the reported understood and said totals, on the reasoning that production implies comprehension. That repaired seven records in which a parent reported more words said than understood, but it did so by overwriting comprehension with the production count — a repair computed from the outcome being modelled, which both removed those records from the source-data violation count the nested likelihood reports and supplied the production likelihood with observations that a child says every word it understands. Those seven records are now handled by the documented policy for a produced count exceeding its comprehension count: retained through the marginal fallback and counted as a source-data violation in the fit log (raising the reported DS violation count from four to eleven).

A related but distinct defect affects six individual us_01 infant administrations, and is handled by an age-conditioned rule rather than a study-specific one. Between 11 and 18 months these six record production within 1–9% of comprehension — 173 to 396 words said — which is internally inconsistent with comprehension leading production, the premise of the joint models' production-ratio decomposition. Three independent lines of evidence identify them as a data-preparation artefact rather than exceptional children. The pattern is rare where it can be checked against a large reference sample: among 2,480 typically-developing Words & Gestures administrations with comprehension of at least 100 words, only 0.69% have production at or above 0.9 of comprehension. The implied production levels are impossible against the independent Down syndrome cohort of @berglundParentalReportsSpoken2001, which places median spoken vocabulary near zero at 12 months and about ten words at 24 months. And each of the three affected children with a second administration shows an ordinary comprehension–production gap in that other record, with ratios of 0.08 to 0.13 against 0.91 to 1.00 in the flagged one; in two of the three, comprehension also falls by 355 and 209 words between the two visits. Because the aggregate data cannot recover which of the two columns was overwritten, both counts are masked and the row is retained. The rule is conditioned on age rather than on source: the same ratio above 18 months describes a child who says most of what they understand, and 21 of the 27 paired records in the pool that meet the ratio and count conditions are of that ordinary kind. Administrations with a high infant comprehension count but a normal production gap are deliberately **not** caught — two us_01 records at 18 months (comprehension 213 and 217, production 31 and 22, at the 48th and 50th typically-developing percentile for comprehension) are retained as clinically unusual rather than invalid, and are a sensitivity target. Item-level responses would settle the mechanism definitively, since a duplicated column appears as two identical response vectors.

Because three separate defects had been found and repaired in this one source by hand, the subset was then audited systematically rather than patched again (`scripts/audit_edgin_subset.py`, which is committed so the audit can be re-run after any later change). The audit enumerates every defect class the aggregate data can expose and found four, affecting 31 of 196 administrations and 30 of 119 children. Two checks came back clean: no count exceeds its form's ceiling, and no form was administered outside its intended age band. Beyond the outcome-column duplication above, the audit identified one administration recorded twice identically — which would otherwise double-weight that observation and make a single-visit child appear to have repeated measures — and two signatures affecting production counts, both scoped to ages at or below 30 months. The first is **saturation at the form maximum**: nineteen administrations at or within a tenth of their form's ceiling, of which thirteen form a contiguous block of consecutive child identifiers, every one at exactly 680 words, with no other administration recorded for any of those children and an eighty-one identifier gap to the next child present. That is a data-preparation signature rather than thirteen exceptionally able children; for comparison, no typically-developing child of 1,469 aged 16 to 19 months reaches the Words & Sentences ceiling, and their maximum is 643. The second is **longitudinal collapse**: a count several-fold larger than the same child's later count, which is unambiguous because vocabulary does not shrink — seven of the eight young ceiling records are contradicted by the same child between twenty-seven and two hundred and twenty-three fold. The collapse rule carries a floor, so that trivial pairs such as five words falling to one do not trigger it, and is scoped by age, because at older ages an apparent decline can follow a form change; two such records in other sources are therefore left for separate investigation rather than masked.

These records were previously treated as valid but right-censored observations, addressed through a registered sensitivity that excluded them. That reading is superseded: they are not censored measurements but invalid values, so they are now excluded by default, and the sensitivity — which could only have excluded records already excluded — has been retired. The live question is the inverse, namely whether the exclusion is itself mistaken, and the data loaders expose it as an option so that it can be tested. Retained by the same logic as the high-comprehension records above is one Words & Sentences count of 406 words at 23 months, extreme against the independent cohort benchmark but with no later administration to contradict it and no positive defect signature.

Wordbank Words & Sentences (WS) records are treated as **production-only** because the WS comprehension field is a production proxy rather than an independent comprehension measurement. TD spoken-only models can use WS production counts, but TD bivariate models that estimate both understood and spoken vocabulary exclude WS rows and rely on WG and Oxford CDI observations for the comprehension-production gap.

The former us_01 Edgin inclusion rule that retained only production counts at or below 100 words has been removed. It had no documented measurement or sampling rationale, excluded 8 of 87 Words & Gestures records and 24 of 109 Words & Sentences records in the 2026-07 export, and conflicted with the source study's use of standard CDI production scores: one Down syndrome subgroup had a reported mean of 275.5 words (SD 198.2) [@edgin2015sleep]. All us_01 counts that satisfy the source-form ceiling guard are therefore retained. Eighteen Words & Sentences records are exactly at that form's 680-word ceiling; these are kept as valid but potentially ceiling-censored observations. The registered `us01-ceiling-excluded` sensitivities for VG10 and VG15 remove exactly those observations so their influence on the principal joint trajectories can be reported explicitly rather than hidden behind an arbitrary threshold.
